catalog_quote: Vorbichler 1967 p. 452: "Tone and stress. (a) By my analysis of Balese it is now firmly established that three distinctive tonemes exist in Mangbutu-Efe. Since then I have got irrefutable proof for their existence in Mamvu, too. (b) Falling tone in long syllables which are virtually disyllabic, occurs also in Balese. In Efe sometimes the sequence [Falling-High] is a variant for Balese /High-High/, while in Mamvu the sequence /Low-Low/ is realized in slow speech as [Low-Rising]. (c) In Balese a long syllable, not being virtually disyllabic, always indicates a stress on the penultimate of a word, word complex, or syntactic unit. One could regard this length as a juncture chroneme." | Vorbichler 1965 §4, §237 (snippets): "Jedoch erhält jeder vorletzte Vokal eines Morphems, einer Morphemzusammensetzung, eines Syntagmas und des Satzes eine gewisse Drucklängung, wobei die letzte Drucklängung …

new_statements.quote: 3. Characteristic features of the tonal system are as follows : (i) Grammatical tone only in verbals, and lexical tones in nominals. (ii) A mid-tone is a slipped high tone occurring between a high and a low tone, or in final position. Recognising this, mid-tones will not subsequently be indicated. (iii) High-falling tone occurs on long vowels before either a high or a low tone on the next syllable. A high-falling tone is marked with the accent ("), a high tone with the accent ('), and a low tone is not accented.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (19 pp., text layer; extracted text). The quoted §3 passage is on extract p. 5 = journal p. 156 (the printed folio "156" sits at the foot of that page), exactly as the locator says. Text matches the report's quote word for word; the only differences are scanned/typography: "nomi-nals" is line-broken in the scan, and the high-falling accent glyph prints as (”) in the scanned where the report has ("). §2 phonetic system (5 vowels, no length contrast in radicals, final-vowel lengthening of disyllabic direct objects) is on p. 155 as stated. new_statements.rule_in_words: Lese (Karo dialect) is described as a tone language: high vs. low tones, with mid as a conditioned (slipped) high and a high-falling tone on long vowels; tone is lexical on nominals and grammatical on verbals. Word stress/accent is never mentioned as a separate property; the 'accent' marks in the source are tone diacritics only.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress (none exists). Tonal notes: mid tones are derived and left unmarked; Obi-dialect forms differ 'both tonally and phonetically' from Karo (p. 155).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone on nominals and verbals, citation and sentence forms of the Karo dialect (informants from Akakora and Alambi, 1954-55). Also notes (p. 155) that a final vowel is lengthened in disyllabic direct objects, a phrase-level length effect, not stress. The 1956 sketch is by a self-declared Bantuist and is superseded by Vorbichler's 1965 full phonology, which could not be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: Harries 1956 describes the Karo dialect of Balese (informants from Akakora and Alambi villages; Obi forms noted as differing tonally); Glottolog lese1243 covers Lese with its Karo, Obi and Dese/Andali varieties, and Vorbichler 1965 is coded by Glottolog as Balese-Obi (Süd-Balese). Efe (efee1239, ISO efe) is the same language per Bahuchet 2006 (not even a distinct dialect) and is what Smith 1938 and Kilian-Hatz 2019 describe.

sources.locator: §3 'Characteristic features of the tonal system', p. 156 (extract pdf p. 5; whole-issue scan pdf p. 66); phonetic system §2 on p. 155
sources.note: Nothing on stress or accent as such. §2 (p.155) phonetic system: 5 vowels, no vowel-length contrast in radicals, final-vowel lengthening of disyllabic direct objects. §3 (p.156) tonal system: grammatical tone in verbals, lexical tone in nominals; mid tone is a slipped high; high-falling on long vowels; only high tones are marked with an acute accent. Karo dialect, informants at Akakora and Alambi, SOAS fieldwork 1954-55; author is a Bantuist.
